raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both full texts are complete and readable, and they are companion reports built on the exact same underlying five-site empirical dataset from Transparency International's Transparency and Integrity in Service Delivery in Africa (TISDA) program (citing GII 2011, TI Kenya 2011, and Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016). Both papers examine the exact same three urban neighborhoods/utilities in Kenya—Old Town in Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi in Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi in Nairobi (NCWSC)—and the exact same two urban neighborhoods in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). They reproduce the same empirical tables and findings: the main WSD actor-role matrix (Study A Table 4 vs Study B Table 5), the participatory Transparency, Accountability and Participation (TAP) scoring rubric and principal-agent relationship scores (Study A Table 1 and Figs. 1–2 vs Study B Tables 7–8), the Water Service Delivery Approach (WSDA) performance scores across the five sites (identical site totals of 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15 in Study A Table 5 and Study B Table 6, with Continuity and Coverage row labels transposed in Study A), and the resulting corruption-risk and opportunistic/pragmatic management classifications across policy/regulation, provision and consumption levels (Study A Table 7 vs Study B Table 9). Study A explicitly cites Study B in manuscript form ('F. Bellaubi and F. Boehm 2016, unpublished manuscript', pp. 3, 12), while Study B (p. 20) points directly to agent-based modeling as the follow-on exploration. Analytically, Study B provides the qualitative institutional 'water control' and governability analysis of the five case studies, whereas Study A uses the same empirical TAP, power-asymmetry and WSDA performance scores to parameterize and calibrate a deterministic 12-month NetLogo 4.1.3 agent-based model; however, any synthesis extracting empirical WSD performance, TAP scores, corruption risks or management practices from both papers would double-count the identical five-case-study sample.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Empirical input and calibration data from 5 urban water service delivery case studies conducted under Transparency International's TISDA program (GII 2011; TIK 2011; Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016): 3 in Kenya—Old Town/Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi/Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi/Nairobi (NCWSC)—and 2 in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). Participatory TAP (transparency, accountability, participation) scores, power/social-cost scores and WSDA user-end performance scores (totals 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15) are used to parameterize and calibrate a deterministic 12-step monthly Agent-Based Model (NetLogo 4.1.3) simulating principal-agent game-theoretic social dilemmas across policy/regulation, provision and consumption levels.
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative institutional, power-asymmetry and governability ('water control') analysis of the exact same 5 urban water service delivery case studies from Transparency International's TISDA program (GII 2011; TI Kenya 2011; Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016): 3 in Kenya—Old Town/Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi/Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi/Nairobi (NCWSC)—and 2 in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). Data derive from formal interviews and informal discussions with public officials, utility managers and technicians, cross-checked with users, informal providers, community groups, donor/NGO staff and internal utility/regulatory documents, summarized via participatory TAP scores (0, 0.5, 1) and WSDA performance scores (totals 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15).
